slides.title: Uprising Against the Jamahiriya
slides.cap: Map of the First Libyan Civil War.
slides.body: Libya's 2011 revolt grew from Arab Spring protests, local anger at repression, and decades of rule by Muammar Gaddafi's security state. Demonstrations spread quickly, the regime used force, and opposition-held cities began organizing armed resistance. The conflict soon became a civil war over whether Gaddafi's system would survive or collapse.

stats.val: Protest movement turns into armed revolt

title: Uprising Begins
sub: Opposition cities break from regime control

markers.label: Benghazi
markers.description: Benghazi became the opposition's main eastern stronghold.

markers.label: Misrata
markers.description: Misrata's resistance later became crucial to the anti-Gaddafi war effort.

slides.title: Cities Become the Revolution's Base
slides.cap: Opposition fighters during the 2011 Libyan Civil War.
slides.body: The uprising began with protests and quickly moved into armed confrontation as security forces fired on demonstrators and local units defected or collapsed. Eastern cities, especially Benghazi, became opposition centers. The speed of the revolt shocked the regime, but the lack of a unified opposition command also foreshadowed the militia fragmentation that would follow victory.

markers.label: Ras Lanuf
markers.description: Oil-coast towns changed hands as regime forces regained momentum.

markers.label: Benghazi
markers.description: The threatened assault on Benghazi drove the international debate over civilian protection.

slides.title: The Revolt Nearly Breaks
slides.cap: Libyan battlefield imagery during the regime counteroffensive.
slides.body: Gaddafi's counteroffensive reversed early rebel gains along the coast and threatened Benghazi. Better-armed regime forces used armor, artillery, aircraft, and loyal units to exploit the opposition's weak organization. The advance made the war's central question immediate: would outside powers allow the regime to retake rebel cities by force, or intervene before Benghazi fell?

markers.label: UN Headquarters
markers.description: The Security Council authorized a no-fly zone and all necessary measures to protect civilians.

markers.label: Benghazi
markers.description: The threat to Benghazi framed the urgency of the vote.

slides.title: A Legal Mandate for Intervention
slides.cap: UN Security Council members during the Libya vote.
slides.body: UN Security Council Resolution 1973 authorized a no-fly zone and the use of all necessary measures to protect civilians, while excluding a foreign occupation force. The resolution gave international legal cover to military action. It also created later controversy because a mission framed around civilian protection helped produce regime change.

stats.val: Civilian protection mandate leads to NATO campaign

markers.label: Benghazi approaches
markers.description: Coalition airstrikes stopped regime forces near Benghazi.

markers.label: Mediterranean air corridor
markers.description: NATO aircraft and ships enforced the no-fly zone and struck regime forces.

slides.title: From No-Fly Zone to Air Campaign
slides.cap: Aircraft imagery representing the NATO-led intervention.
slides.body: Western and NATO intervention began with strikes against Libyan air defenses and regime forces threatening Benghazi. The campaign prevented an immediate rebel defeat, then evolved into sustained air support that weakened Gaddafi's military across the country. Airpower changed the balance, but it could not by itself build a unified postwar state.

stats.val: Air campaign shifts momentum to the opposition

markers.label: Tripoli
markers.description: Opposition fighters entered the capital in August 2011, collapsing Gaddafi's central authority.

markers.label: Bab al-Aziziya
markers.description: The capture of Gaddafi's compound symbolized the fall of the regime.

slides.title: The Capital Falls
slides.cap: A Libyan rebel walks near damaged regime symbols in Tripoli.
slides.body: The fall of Tripoli broke the regime's political center. Rebel forces entered the city with support from local uprisings and NATO pressure, while Gaddafi's command structure unraveled. The victory was decisive for the dictatorship, but it also exposed the opposition's central weakness: many armed groups could defeat the regime, yet no single authority could easily control them afterward.

stats.val: Regime center collapses before state authority is rebuilt

title: Gaddafi Killed at Sirte
sub: The dictator's death ends organized regime resistance

markers.label: Sirte
markers.description: Gaddafi was captured and killed near Sirte after his convoy was struck and surrounded.

markers.label: Coastal escape route
markers.description: The convoy's failed escape showed the regime had lost operational space.

slides.title: The End of Gaddafi
slides.cap: France 24 image associated with Gaddafi's capture.
slides.body: Muammar Gaddafi was captured and killed near Sirte after the collapse of his final stronghold. His death ended organized loyalist resistance and gave the revolution a clear symbolic victory. It did not end Libya's crisis. Weapons, militias, local rivalries, and weak institutions remained, turning victory into a difficult and unstable transition.

stats.val: Regime defeat does not resolve militia fragmentation

markers.label: Libyan coast
markers.description: NATO ended its air and maritime mission after Gaddafi's death and the fall of loyalist strongholds.

markers.label: Tripoli
markers.description: The new authorities inherited the capital without a monopoly on force.

slides.title: The Intervention Ends Before the Aftermath Is Solved
slides.cap: Al Jazeera image from the end of NATO's Libya mission.
slides.body: NATO ended Operation Unified Protector on 31 October 2011. The mission had helped protect opposition-held cities and destroy much of Gaddafi's military capability. Its ending exposed the harder political problem: Libya had no strong security institutions ready to absorb militias, secure weapons, or create a durable national settlement.

stats.val: Military success leaves unresolved state-building problem

title: Conflict Summary: First Libyan Civil War
sub: Victory, intervention, and the unstable aftermath

markers.label: Benghazi
markers.description: The revolt's eastern base survived because local resistance and foreign intervention stopped the regime counteroffensive.

markers.label: Tripoli
markers.description: The capital's fall ended Gaddafi's rule but did not create a unified postwar security order.

markers.label: Sirte
markers.description: Gaddafi's death at Sirte closed the war's regime-change phase.

slides.title: What the War Changed
slides.cap: Libya and NATO imagery from the 2011 war's aftermath.
slides.body: The First Libyan Civil War overthrew Gaddafi and prevented the immediate destruction of the opposition, but it did not produce a stable postwar order. The deep dive's central lesson is the gap between battlefield success and political settlement. Airpower, rebel courage, and diplomatic action could defeat the regime; building a state after the regime collapsed proved far harder.

stats.val: Unstable transition leads toward renewed conflict
